quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "weekend trip" quickly. The consonants pile up right around the /d/ in "weekend" — does it survive the crowd, or get squeezed out?
quests.explanation: When /d/ sits between two other consonants, English speakers routinely drop it to keep the rhythm smooth. In "weekend trip", the /d/ disappears rather than being pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ at the end of "good" is about to meet a bilabial sound in "price". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a bilabial consonant, /d/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "good price", /d/ becomes /b/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "bad part" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /d/ stay a /d/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /d/ ending "bad" turns into /b/ because "part" begins with a bilabial consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A velar consonant is coming up in "gap". What does that do to the /d/ just before it in "wide"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /d/ anticipate the velar sound ahead. So in "wide gap", /d/ is pronounced as /g/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant cluster forming between "adjust" and "volume". In natural speech, one sound in that cluster usually disappears. Which one?
quests.explanation: Three consonants in a row are hard to articulate cleanly, so speakers simplify by deleting the middle one. That's exactly what happens to the /t/ in "adjust volume" — it's dropped, not just softened.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /d/ at the end of "told". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "stories"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /d/ at the end of "told" disappears before the consonant that starts "stories".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /n/ ending "ten" to the bilabial sound that opens "meals". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /n/ becomes /m/ in "ten meals" to match the bilabial consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "hit" to "goal". Is it still /t/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /t/ meets a velar sound, the /t/ shifts to /k/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "hit goal".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "what" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the velar sound in "colour"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a velar position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /k/ in "what colour".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "must finish" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /t/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "must finish", the /t/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "good". With a bilabial consonant starting "match" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /d/ ending "good" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /d/ becomes /b/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "match".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /d/ where "send" meets "text" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /d/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "send text" aloud and you'll notice the /d/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "best" get pronounced before "news", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "best" is the one that goes missing before "news".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Picture how a native speaker would say "missed lunch" in a fast, everyday sentence. Is every single consonant still there?
quests.explanation: This is a textbook case of consonant-cluster elision: the /t/ between two consonants is dropped to keep speech fluent and effortless in "missed lunch".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ in "connect" is trapped between two other consonants right before "now". What usually happens to a stop consonant stuck in that position?
quests.explanation: Rather than pronounce all three consonants back to back, speakers cut the /t/ from "connect" entirely. The result flows straight from the first consonant into "now".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen closely at the boundary of "beyond" and "doubt" — count the consonants stacking up. Does the /d/ still make it into the sentence?
quests.explanation: In fast, connected speech, a /d/ wedged between consonants almost always disappears. That's what you'll hear in "beyond doubt" — the /d/ goes silent.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "best price" naturally, without pausing between the words. Is the /t/ audible, or does it disappear into the next consonant?

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "that movie" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /t/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /t/ rarely stays /t/ before a bilabial sound — it assimilates to /p/, which is exactly what you hear in "that movie".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This pair, "locked door", creates a tricky consonant sequence. Which sound do fluent speakers simplify away — and is it really gone, or just quieter?
quests.explanation: Speakers naturally avoid three consonants in a row, so the /t/ is dropped rather than forced through. That's why "locked door" sounds smoother without it.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Fluent speech avoids awkward consonant pile-ups. Where exactly does that simplification happen in "mild weather"?
quests.explanation: This cluster is simplified by deleting the /d/ altogether — not weakening it, not shifting it, just leaving it out — which is the defining feature of elision in "mild weather".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "swept" alone, then "clean" alone — both consonants are clear. Now blend them at speed. What happens to the /t/ in between?
quests.explanation: Notice that nothing replaces the /t/ — it isn't weakened or swapped for another sound, it's simply omitted. That full deletion is what separates elision from assimilation in "swept clean".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE

quests.explanation: The change from /n/ to /m/ at the end of "ten" happens because the following bilabial consonant in "pencils" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.
